claim: Biodiversity increases ecosystem functions underpinning a suite of services valued by society, including services provided by soils.
source: Biodiversity increases ecosystem functions underpinning a suite of services valued by society, including services provided by soils.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: Plant diversity increased three out of four soil functions.
source: Our results showed that plant diversity increased three out of four soil functions and, consequently, ecosystem multifunctionality.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Plant diversity increased ecosystem multifunctionality.
source: Our results showed that plant diversity increased three out of four soil functions and, consequently, ecosystem multifunctionality.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Biodiversity-ecosystem function relationships were similarly significant under current and future environmental conditions.
source: Remarkably, biodiversity-ecosystem function relationships were similarly significant under current and future environmental conditions, yet weaker with enriched N supply.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data across different environmental treatments.

claim: Biodiversity-ecosystem function relationships were weaker with enriched N supply.
source: Remarkably, biodiversity-ecosystem function relationships were similarly significant under current and future environmental conditions, yet weaker with enriched N supply.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Plant diversity enhanced ecosystem multifunctionality by increasing plant community functional diversity.
source: Structural equation models revealed that plant diversity enhanced ecosystem multifunctionality by increasing plant community functional diversity, and the even provision of multiple functions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding stated in the abstract and supported by structural equation modeling.

claim: Plant diversity enhanced ecosystem multifunctionality by increasing the even provision of multiple functions.
source: Structural equation models revealed that plant diversity enhanced ecosystem multifunctionality by increasing plant community functional diversity, and the even provision of multiple functions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding stated in the abstract and supported by structural equation modeling.

claim: Conserving local plant diversity is a robust strategy to maintain multiple valuable ecosystem services in both present and future environmental conditions.
source: Conserving local plant diversity is therefore a robust strategy to maintain multiple valuable ecosystem services in both present and future environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Both the average levels and temporal stability of ecosystem functions increase with biodiversity.
source: Many experimental studies have shown that both the average levels (Hooper et al., 2005; Cardinale et al., 2012; Duffy et al., 2017) and temporal stability (Isbell et al., 2015) of ecosystem functions increase with biodiversity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The generality of positive relationships between biodiversity and ecosystem functioning is well established.
source: While the generality of positive relationships between biodiversity and ecosystem functioning is well established (Cardinale et al., 2012; Duffy et al., 2017; Isbell et al., 2015; Lefcheck et al., 2015), current research focuses on the underlying mechanisms (Eisenhauer et al., 2016; Zuppinger-Dingley et al., 2014; Laforest-Lapointe et al., 2017) and context-dependencies (Craven et al., 2016; Guerrero-Ramírez et al., 2017) of biodiversity-ecosystem function relationships, given that ecosystems face progressive environmental changes (Barros and IPCC. Climate Change, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Different species complement or facilitate each other in chemical, spatial, and temporal resource use, resulting in higher functional diversity.
source: One of the most prominent explanations of why diverse communities perform better than simple ones is that different species complement or facilitate each other in chemical, spatial, and temporal resource use (Loreau and Hector, 2001; Eisenhauer, 2012), resulting in higher functional diversity.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Diverse communities may have higher functioning because of an elevated probability of containing and becoming dominated by one or a few productive species.
source: Alternatively, diverse communities may have higher functioning because of an elevated probability of containing and becoming dominated by one or a few productive species (Loreau and Hector, 2001).
evidence: This is an alternative mechanistic explanation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Biotic interactions across trophic levels are important drivers of biodiversity effects.
source: Moreover, there is growing evidence that biotic interactions across trophic levels are important drivers of biodiversity effects (Maron et al., 2011; Schnitzer et al., 2011; Eisenhauer et al., 2012a) and that these interactions are significantly modulated by environmental conditions (Guerrero-Ramírez and Eisenhauer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Biotic interactions across trophic levels are significantly modulated by environmental conditions.
source: Moreover, there is growing evidence that biotic interactions across trophic levels are important drivers of biodiversity effects (Maron et al., 2011; Schnitzer et al., 2011; Eisenhauer et al., 2012a) and that these interactions are significantly modulated by environmental conditions (Guerrero-Ramírez and Eisenhauer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Biodiversity effects may depend on the environmental context, such as climatic conditions and resource availability.
source: As a consequence, biodiversity effects may depend on the environmental context, such as climatic conditions and resource availability (Craven et al., 2016; Guerrero-Ramírez et al., 2017), and thus may change in future environments.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents a logical inference from the previous statement.

claim: Studies testing biodiversity-ecosystem function relationships under future conditions are rare.
source: However, studies testing biodiversity-ecosystem function relationships under future conditions are rare (Reich et al., 2001; He et al., 2002; Hooper et al., 2012; Thakur et al., 2015), and typically investigate only one or a few ecosystem functions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and identifies a research gap.

claim: Soils provide many ecosystem functions that contribute to human well-being, including resources that support plant biomass production, such as nutrients and water, soil carbon storage, and soil erosion control.
source: Soils provide many ecosystem functions (Bardgett and van der Putten, 2014) that contribute to human well-being, including resources that support plant biomass production, such as nutrients and water, soil carbon storage, and soil erosion control (Wall et al., 2015; Amundson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Changes in plant diversity have been identified as a key factor influencing soil organisms.
source: Changes in plant diversity have been identified as a key factor influencing soil organisms (Hooper et al., 2000; Scherber et al., 2010; Eisenhauer et al., 2013; Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Diverse plant communities provide a higher quantity and quality of plant-derived inputs to soil microorganisms and detritivores.
source: Through bottom-up effects, diverse plant communities provide a higher quantity and quality of plant-derived inputs to soil microorganisms and detritivores (Hooper et al., 2000; Eisenhauer et al., 2013), which has cascading effects on the abundance and diversity at higher trophic levels in the soil (Hooper et al., 2000; Scherber et al., 2010; Eisenhauer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Diverse plant communities have cascading effects on the abundance and diversity at higher trophic levels in the soil.
source: Through bottom-up effects, diverse plant communities provide a higher quantity and quality of plant-derived inputs to soil microorganisms and detritivores (Hooper et al., 2000; Eisenhauer et al., 2013), which has cascading effects on the abundance and diversity at higher trophic levels in the soil (Hooper et al., 2000; Scherber et al., 2010; Eisenhauer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ecosystem functions mediated by soil organisms, such as soil carbon storage, litter decomposition, and soil aggregate stabilization, are sensitive to changes in the diversity of plant communities.
source: Ecosystem functions mediated by soil organisms, such as soil carbon storage (Lange et al., 2015; Fornara and Tilman, 2008), litter decomposition (Vogel et al., 2013), and soil aggregate stabilization (Gould et al., 2016), are thus sensitive to changes in the diversity of plant communities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Future environmental conditions may alter the relationship between biodiversity and ecosystem multifunctionality.
source: Future environmental conditions may alter the relationship between biodiversity and ecosystem multifunctionality (Manning et al., 2018; Hector and Bagchi, 2007; Soliveres et al., 2016; Byrnes et al., 2014), potentially in distinct ways depending on the response of plant species abundances, or evenness, to new conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Different plant species promote different ecosystem functions.
source: There is considerable evidence that different plant species promote different ecosystem functions (Hector and Bagchi, 2007), and that different plant species provide different ecosystem functions under different global change scenarios (Isbell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Different plant species provide different ecosystem functions under different global change scenarios.
source: There is considerable evidence that different plant species promote different ecosystem functions (Hector and Bagchi, 2007), and that different plant species provide different ecosystem functions under different global change scenarios (Isbell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Resource additions often favor 'fast' (i.e. acquisitive) plant strategies, thereby decreasing the evenness, functional diversity, and species richness of plant communities.
source: Resource additions often favor 'fast' (i.e. acquisitive) plant strategies, thereby decreasing the evenness, functional diversity, and species richness of plant communities (Reich, 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Elevated CO2 concentrations and N addition have been reported to enhance plant diversity effects on plant biomass production.
source: For example, elevated CO2 concentrations and N addition have been reported to enhance plant diversity effects on plant biomass production (Reich et al., 2001) and soil microbial biomass (Eisenhauer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Elevated CO2 concentrations and N addition have been reported to enhance plant diversity effects on soil microbial biomass.
source: For example, elevated CO2 concentrations and N addition have been reported to enhance plant diversity effects on plant biomass production (Reich et al., 2001) and soil microbial biomass (Eisenhauer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The study measured root biomass, soil respiration, soil microbial biomass, and water-stable soil aggregates in 315 plots, 17 years after establishment of the experimental treatments.
source: Here, we report root biomass, soil respiration, soil microbial biomass, and water-stable soil aggregates (representing key functions being altered in disturbed soils) (Amundson et al., 2015), correlations among these functions, as well as ecosystem multifunctionality (Hector and Bagchi, 2007; Byrnes et al., 2014) in a long-term grassland plant diversity experiment, with orthogonal manipulation of atmospheric CO2 concentrations and soil N availability in Minnesota, USA (the BioCON experiment) (Reich et al., 2001). We measured soil functions in 315 plots, 17 years after establishment of the experimental treatments.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and measurements.

claim: Plant root biomass increased significantly with plant diversity.
source: Plant root biomass, soil respiration, and soil microbial biomass C increased significantly with plant diversity, while the percentage of water-stable soil aggregates increased with plant diversity but only with marginal statistical significance (Table 1, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: Soil respiration increased significantly with plant diversity.
source: Plant root biomass, soil respiration, and soil microbial biomass C increased significantly with plant diversity, while the percentage of water-stable soil aggregates increased with plant diversity but only with marginal statistical significance (Table 1, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: Soil microbial biomass C increased significantly with plant diversity.
source: Plant root biomass, soil respiration, and soil microbial biomass C increased significantly with plant diversity, while the percentage of water-stable soil aggregates increased with plant diversity but only with marginal statistical significance (Table 1, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: The percentage of water-stable soil aggregates increased with plant diversity but only with marginal statistical significance.
source: Plant root biomass, soil respiration, and soil microbial biomass C increased significantly with plant diversity, while the percentage of water-stable soil aggregates increased with plant diversity but only with marginal statistical significance (Table 1, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: The identity of top-performing plant species in monoculture depended upon both the response variable and environmental context.
source: The identity of top-performing plant species in monoculture depended upon both the response variable and environmental context (Table S1), indicating that different species provide different functions under different conditions.
evidence: This is a finding supported by data in a supplementary table.

claim: There were no significant interaction effects between plant diversity and global change agents on any individual ecosystem function.
source: Yet, results for community functioning were independent of the environmental context, as there were no significant interaction effects between plant diversity and global change agents on any individual ecosystem function.
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis.

claim: None of the global change treatments had a significant effect on the single-soil functions.
source: In contrast to plant diversity, none of the global change treatments had a significant effect on the single-soil functions (Table 1, Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: A significant proportion of soil respiration was associated with microbial biomass C (r² = 0.45).
source: As an exception, a significant proportion of soil respiration was associated with microbial biomass C (r² = 0.45; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by correlation analysis and figure.

claim: The individual soil functions were generally not, or only weakly correlated with each other across the environmental contexts (in five out of the six possible correlations between soil functions r2 ≤0.1).
source: Despite the consistent linear relationships between plant diversity and the soil functions (Figure 1), the individual soil functions were generally not, or only weakly correlated with each other across the environmental contexts (in five out of the six possible correlations between soil functions r2 ≤0.1; Figure 2; note that Pearson's correlation coefficients (r) are shown in Figure 2, while we refer to r² values in the text).
evidence: This is a finding supported by correlation analysis and figure.

claim: Average ecosystem multifunctionality responded strongly to variations in plant diversity, increasing by 40% from monocultures to 16-species mixtures.
source: Average ecosystem multifunctionality responded strongly to variations in plant diversity, increasing by 40% from monocultures to 16-species mixtures.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The strong plant diversity effect on ecosystem multifunctionality was independent of the global change treatments.
source: The strong plant diversity effect on ecosystem multifunctionality was independent of the global change treatments (Table 1, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and figure.

claim: CO2 and N enrichment or their interactive effects with plant diversity on multifunctionality were not significant.
source: In contrast to strong plant diversity effects, CO2 and N enrichment or their interactive effects with plant diversity on multifunctionality were not significant (Table 1, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and figure.

claim: As the threshold for performance increased from 20 to 80%, plant communities were able to support fewer functions above threshold values.
source: As the threshold for performance increased from 20 to 80%, plant communities were able to support fewer functions above threshold values and the influence of diversity on multiple ecosystem functions was more strongly contingent upon environmental conditions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the multiple threshold analysis and figure.

claim: The influence of diversity on multiple ecosystem functions was more strongly contingent upon environmental conditions as the threshold for performance increased from 20 to 80%.
source: As the threshold for performance increased from 20 to 80%, plant communities were able to support fewer functions above threshold values and the influence of diversity on multiple ecosystem functions was more strongly contingent upon environmental conditions (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by the multiple threshold analysis and figure.

claim: At the 20% and 40% thresholds, the interaction between CO2 and N was significant.
source: At the 20% and 40% thresholds, the interaction between CO2 and N was significant (Table 1), with more functions performed above thresholds in ambient conditions and in conditions with both elevated CO2 and elevated N (an effect that was also observed for 60% thresholds), and fewer functions performed above the threshold in conditions of elevated CO2 and elevated N in isolation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and figure.

claim: For the 60% and 80% thresholds, plant species richness effects on the number of functions delivered above the threshold level were strongest under ambient conditions.
source: For the 60% and 80% thresholds, plant species richness effects on the number of functions delivered above the threshold level were strongest under ambient conditions, and the weakest effects were observed under elevated N conditions (significant plant species richness × CO2×N effect; Table 1, Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and figure.

claim: For the 60% and 80% thresholds, the weakest plant species richness effects on the number of functions delivered above the threshold level were observed under elevated N conditions.
source: For the 60% and 80% thresholds, plant species richness effects on the number of functions delivered above the threshold level were strongest under ambient conditions, and the weakest effects were observed under elevated N conditions (significant plant species richness × CO2×N effect; Table 1, Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and figure.

claim: Sown plant species richness increased realized species richness.
source: Sown plant species richness increased realized species richness, the Shannon diversity, evenness, and the functional diversity of the plant community (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and table.

claim: Sown plant species richness increased the Shannon diversity of the plant community.
source: Sown plant species richness increased realized species richness, the Shannon diversity, evenness, and the functional diversity of the plant community (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and table.

claim: Sown plant species richness increased evenness of the plant community.
source: Sown plant species richness increased realized species richness, the Shannon diversity, evenness, and the functional diversity of the plant community (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and table.

claim: Sown plant species richness increased the functional diversity of the plant community.
source: Sown plant species richness increased realized species richness, the Shannon diversity, evenness, and the functional diversity of the plant community (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and table.

claim: The increase in realized diversity with increasing sown plant species richness tended to be less pronounced in the elevated CO2 and N treatments.
source: Overall, however, this increase in realized diversity with increasing sown plant species richness tended to be less pronounced in the elevated CO2 and N treatments (significant plant species richness × environmental change effects in Table 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; this pattern was consistent across plant community diversity and functional diversity indices, Figure 4—figure supplements 2–5).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: Plant species richness increased the Shannon diversity of multiple soil functions.
source: Plant species richness increased the Shannon diversity and evenness of multiple soil functions (i.e. the Shannon evenness index of the four standardized soil function values), while CO2 and N as well as interactions among the three factors did not significantly influence these soil responses (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and table.

claim: Plant species richness increased the evenness of multiple soil functions.
source: Plant species richness increased the Shannon diversity and evenness of multiple soil functions (i.e. the Shannon evenness index of the four standardized soil function values), while CO2 and N as well as interactions among the three factors did not significantly influence these soil responses (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and table.

claim: CO2 and N as well as interactions among the three factors did not significantly influence the Shannon diversity and evenness of multiple soil functions.
source: Plant species richness increased the Shannon diversity and evenness of multiple soil functions (i.e. the Shannon evenness index of the four standardized soil function values), while CO2 and N as well as interactions among the three factors did not significantly influence these soil responses (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and table.

claim: The positive effect of plant species richness on ecosystem multifunctionality could be explained by increased plant community functional diversity and evenness of multiple soil functions at high plant diversity.
source: Moreover, structural equation models (SEMs) revealed that the positive effect of plant species richness on ecosystem multifunctionality could be explained by increased plant community functional diversity and evenness of multiple soil functions at high plant diversity (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding supported by structural equation modeling and figure.

claim: No direct paths between plant species richness and ecosystem multifunctionality were supported by the SEM.
source: No direct paths between plant species richness and ecosystem multifunctionality were supported by the SEM, indicating that plant species richness effects on ecosystem multifunctionality were fully explained by changes in the functional diversity of the plant community and evenness of ecosystem multifunctionality.
evidence: This is a finding from structural equation modeling.

claim: Plant species richness effects on ecosystem multifunctionality were fully explained by changes in the functional diversity of the plant community and evenness of ecosystem multifunctionality.
source: No direct paths between plant species richness and ecosystem multifunctionality were supported by the SEM, indicating that plant species richness effects on ecosystem multifunctionality were fully explained by changes in the functional diversity of the plant community and evenness of ecosystem multifunctionality.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion from structural equation modeling.

claim: CO2 and N were not retained in the final SEM.
source: Although several significant interaction effects for plant species richness × CO2 (Shannon diversity, Shannon evenness, functional dispersion) and plant species richness × N (realized species richness, Shannon diversity, Shannon evenness, Simpson evenness, functional dispersion) on the plant community were observed (Table 2), CO2 and N were not retained in the final SEM (removal of non-significant paths improved the model fit based on AIC).
evidence: This is a finding from structural equation modeling.

claim: Strong plant species richness effects overrode any CO2 and N effects on plant community evenness, functional diversity, and evenness of multiple soil functions in driving ecosystem multifunctionality.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that strong plant species richness effects overrode any CO2 and N effects on plant community evenness, functional diversity, and evenness of multiple soil functions in driving ecosystem multifunctionality (Table 1, Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural equation modeling and statistical analyses.

claim: Significant plant diversity effects on multiple soil functions, and therefore ecosystem multifunctionality, are largely robust to changes in environmental conditions caused by elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations, N inputs, and both factors in combination.
source: Our study shows the first empirical evidence that significant plant diversity effects on multiple soil functions, and therefore ecosystem multifunctionality, are largely robust to changes in environmental conditions caused by elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations, N inputs, and both factors in combination.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Plant diversity effects on ecosystem multifunctionality at higher thresholds of functionality may be impaired under future environmental conditions.
source: However, plant diversity effects on ecosystem multifunctionality at higher thresholds of functionality may be impaired under future environmental conditions (Figure 4), potentially by reducing the taxonomic and functional diversity of the plant community (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the multiple threshold analysis and figures.

claim: Plant diversity effects on ecosystem multifunctionality were mediated by higher levels of plant community functional diversity and the more even provisioning of multiple soil functions.
source: Plant diversity effects on ecosystem multifunctionality were mediated by higher levels of plant community functional diversity and the more even provisioning of multiple soil functions.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion supported by structural equation modeling.

claim: Root biomass, soil respiration, soil microbial biomass C, and percentage of water-stable soil aggregates are indicators of belowground plant biomass production, organic matter decomposition, soil carbon storage, and soil erosion control, respectively.
source: Our measurements of root biomass, soil respiration, soil microbial biomass C, and percentage of water-stable soil aggregates are indicators of belowground plant biomass production, organic matter decomposition, soil carbon storage (Lange et al., 2015), and soil erosion control, respectively, which denote some of the most crucial ecosystem services grasslands provide for human well-being (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and established knowledge.

claim: Management policies targeted to maximize these services through maintaining or increasing plant diversity should be applicable under a wide range of contexts.
source: Thus, management policies targeted to maximize these services through maintaining or increasing plant diversity should be applicable under a wide range of contexts (Manning et al., 2018), although high availability of certain resources may compromise beneficial plant diversity effects on high levels of functioning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings with citation support.

claim: High availability of certain resources may compromise beneficial plant diversity effects on high levels of functioning.
source: Thus, management policies targeted to maximize these services through maintaining or increasing plant diversity should be applicable under a wide range of contexts (Manning et al., 2018), although high availability of certain resources may compromise beneficial plant diversity effects on high levels of functioning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The composition, species richness, and functioning (e.g. plant biomass production) of grasslands can be significantly affected by anthropogenic environmental changes, such as climate change, elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations, and N deposition.
source: Previous studies, including from this field experiment (Reich, 2009), have shown that the composition, species richness, and functioning (e.g. plant biomass production) of grasslands can be significantly affected by anthropogenic environmental changes, such as climate change (Reich et al., 2014b; Grime et al., 2000), elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations (Reich et al., 2001; Morgan et al., 2011), and N deposition (Clark and Tilman, 2008; Simkin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Elevated CO2 concentrations and N input had no significant effects on soil functions.
source: In contrast, in the present study, elevated CO2 concentrations and N input had no significant effects on soil functions (Table 1), despite significantly increased aboveground plant biomass in the N addition treatment (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and tables.

claim: N addition significantly increased aboveground plant biomass.
source: In contrast, in the present study, elevated CO2 concentrations and N input had no significant effects on soil functions (Table 1), despite significantly increased aboveground plant biomass in the N addition treatment (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and table.

claim: The response of grassland functions to environmental change depends on local conditions like precedent climate events and history of anthropogenic disturbances.
source: These overall weak or missing effects might be because the response of grassland functions to environmental change depends on local conditions like precedent climate events and history of anthropogenic disturbances (Grime et al., 2000; Simkin et al., 2016), although we did not record any particularly harsh environmental conditions in the year of the study.
evidence: This is a potential explanation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous research in the BioCON experiment showed significant CO2 and N effects on plant biomass and total belowground carbon allocation, as well as on soil communities and functions.
source: Previous research in the BioCON experiment showed significant CO2 and N effects on plant biomass (Reich et al., 2001) and total belowground carbon allocation, as well as on soil communities (He et al., 2010; Eisenhauer et al., 2012b) and functions (Chung et al., 2007; Reich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research from the same experiment.

claim: The effect of global change drivers on total belowground carbon allocation and soil functions may increase or decrease over time and vary among years and species compositions alone or jointly.
source: However, the effect of those global change drivers on total belowground carbon allocation and soil functions may increase or decrease over time and vary among years and species compositions alone or jointly (Reich et al., 2018; Adair et al., 2009; Andresen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: High-diversity plant communities are more likely to include different root traits, that is deep- and shallow-rooting species, than low-diversity communities.
source: In line with other studies (Reich et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2013; Ravenek et al., 2014), we observed positive effects of plant diversity on root biomass. High-diversity plant communities are more likely to include different root traits, that is deep- and shallow-rooting species, than low-diversity communities (Mueller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Higher diversity plant communities have been shown to increase root biomass in surface soils and the proportion of deep roots.
source: Thereby, higher diversity plant communities have been shown to increase root biomass in surface soils (Ravenek et al., 2014) and the proportion of deep roots (Mueller et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased plant biomass production at high plant diversity (above and below the ground) and increased diversity of organic inputs to the soil have been shown to enhance soil microbial biomass and activity.
source: Increased plant biomass production at high plant diversity (above and below the ground) and increased diversity of organic inputs to the soil have been shown to enhance soil microbial biomass and activity (Hooper et al., 2000; Eisenhauer et al., 2013; Lange et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Elevated microbial activity, such as indicated by soil respiration, reflects the transfer of higher amounts of plant products into microbial products that then accumulate in the soil.
source: However, these results are in line with recent findings showing that elevated microbial activity, such as indicated by soil respiration, reflects the transfer of higher amounts of plant products into microbial products that then accumulate in the soil (Lange et al., 2015; Cotrufo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Although high soil respiration means greater short-term losses of organic matter as CO2, it can also indicate enhanced long-term soil carbon storage.
source: Thus, although high soil respiration means greater short-term losses of organic matter as CO2, it can also indicate enhanced long-term soil carbon storage (Lange et al., 2015; Cotrufo et al., 2015) as microbial necromass might end up in slow-cycling soil organic matter pools (Cotrufo et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Microbial necromass might end up in slow-cycling soil organic matter pools.
source: Thus, although high soil respiration means greater short-term losses of organic matter as CO2, it can also indicate enhanced long-term soil carbon storage (Lange et al., 2015; Cotrufo et al., 2015) as microbial necromass might end up in slow-cycling soil organic matter pools (Cotrufo et al., 2015; Schmidt et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The proportion of water-stable soil aggregates did not significantly increase with plant diversity, root biomass, microbial biomass, elevated CO2, or N addition.
source: In contrast to previous studies, the proportion of water-stable soil aggregates did not significantly increase with plant diversity (Gould et al., 2016; Pérès et al., 2013), root biomass (Gould et al., 2016), microbial biomass (Gould et al., 2016; Pérès et al., 2013), elevated CO2 (Rillig et al., 2001), or N addition (Riggs et al., 2015), although positive trends were observed with diversity (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis, figure, and contrasted with citations to previous research.

claim: Soil aggregate stability contributes to the regulating ecosystem service soil erosion control.
source: Soil aggregate stability contributes to the regulating ecosystem service soil erosion control (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, 2005), which is of major relevance in a rapidly changing world with increased likelihood of extreme weather events (Amundson et al., 2015; Fischer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and established knowledge.

claim: Soil aggregate stability informs soil carbon storage, as aggregates incorporate organic matter protecting it from decomposition on decadal timescales.
source: Soil aggregate stability also informs soil carbon storage, as aggregates incorporate organic matter protecting it from decomposition (Six et al., 2000) on decadal timescales.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Soil aggregate stability depends on soil biological properties, such as (fine) root biomass and root length density, and soil biota including microbes and animals.
source: Although soil aggregate stability depends on soil biological properties, such as (fine) root biomass and root length density (Gould et al., 2016), and soil biota including microbes and animals (Lehmann et al., 2017), abiotic factors like soil texture are also important controls (Denef et al., 2002) and may have prevailed in the very sandy soil of the present study (Reich et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Abiotic factors like soil texture are important controls of soil aggregate stability and may have prevailed in the very sandy soil of the present study.
source: Although soil aggregate stability depends on soil biological properties, such as (fine) root biomass and root length density (Gould et al., 2016), and soil biota including microbes and animals (Lehmann et al., 2017), abiotic factors like soil texture are also important controls (Denef et al., 2002) and may have prevailed in the very sandy soil of the present study (Reich et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a potential explanation supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Elevated resources can facilitate the dominance of certain species that are more efficient in resource use leading to reduced taxonomic and functional diversity of plant communities.
source: Elevated resources can facilitate the dominance of certain species that are more efficient in resource use leading to reduced taxonomic and functional diversity of plant communities (Morgan et al., 2011; Clark and Tilman, 2008; Simkin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Elevated resource availability decreased realized plant species richness, community evenness, and functional diversity in the present study.
source: Indeed, elevated resource availability decreased realized plant species richness, community evenness, and functional diversity in the present study (Table 2, Figure 4—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This is a finding supported by statistical analysis and figures.

claim: Higher sown plant diversity attenuated the detrimental effects of elevated resource availability on realized plant diversity indices.
